concepts.name: Definition and Legal Status of Payments Banks
key_dimensions: Differentiated bank license vs. universal bank license — what 'differentiated' means in RBI's licensing framework
Governed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — same parent law as commercial banks, a common UPSC trap
Nachiket Mor Committee (2013) recommendation as the origin — linking committee to policy outcome
Distinction from Cooperative Banks and RRBs — overlapping confusion in exam questions

concepts.name: Eligible Promoters and Licensing Criteria
key_dimensions: Categories eligible: prepaid payment instrument issuers, telecom companies, supermarket chains, NBFCs, corporates, individuals, NGOs — breadth of eligibility is a frequent MCQ trap
Minimum paid-up equity capital requirement: Rs. 100 crore — comparison with Small Finance Banks (Rs. 200 crore) is a classic UPSC trap
Promoter's minimum initial contribution: 40% for first 5 years — lock-in period nuance
Foreign shareholding permitted as per FDI policy for private banks — often overlooked angle

concepts.name: Deposit Acceptance Limits and Restrictions
key_dimensions: Maximum balance per individual customer: Rs. 2 lakh (revised from Rs. 1 lakh in 2021) — the revision itself is a high-yield fact
Can accept demand deposits (savings and current accounts) but CANNOT accept time deposits/fixed deposits — critical 'cannot do' restriction
No NRI deposits allowed — explicit prohibition, a common trap against regular banks
Comparison with Small Finance Banks which have no such ceiling on deposits

concepts.name: Prohibition on Lending Activities
key_dimensions: Cannot issue loans or credit cards — the most fundamental restriction differentiating payments banks
Cannot advance loans including consumer credit, mortgages, or business loans
Implication: payments banks are 'narrow banks' by design — concept of narrow banking linkage
Cannot set up subsidiaries to undertake NBFC activities — subsidiary restriction often missed

concepts.name: Permitted Investment Activities and SLR Requirements
key_dimensions: Minimum 75% of demand deposit balances must be invested in SLR-eligible government securities/treasury bills with maturity up to one year — the '75% rule' is highly specific and examinable
Maximum 25% can be held as current and time/fixed deposits with other scheduled commercial banks — the parking mechanism
This makes payments banks inherently low-risk but low-return institutions
Comparison with SLR requirements for commercial banks (currently ~18%) to highlight the stricter norm

concepts.name: Payment and Remittance Services Allowed
key_dimensions: Can issue ATM/debit cards but NOT credit cards — the debit-yes/credit-no distinction
Can provide internet banking, mobile banking, and payment gateway services
Can handle domestic remittances (Person-to-Person transfers) — key permitted service
Permitted to be a Business Correspondent (BC) of another bank — allows indirect credit facilitation, a nuanced overlap

concepts.name: Payments Banks as Business Correspondents (BC) of Other Banks
key_dimensions: Payments banks CAN act as BCs for commercial banks — this indirectly enables credit access to their customers
This blurs the line between 'no lending' restriction and actual credit delivery on ground
Distinction: acting as BC is a fee-based service, not on-balance-sheet lending
Policy rationale: last-mile credit delivery without exposing payments bank balance sheet to credit risk

concepts.name: Capital Adequacy and Prudential Norms
key_dimensions: Minimum Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR): 15% — higher than the 10.875% norm for commercial banks, a key comparative fact
Leverage ratio requirements apply as per Basel III framework
Since no loans, credit risk is minimal — but operational and liquidity risk management remains critical
RBI's supervisory framework: payments banks fall under RBI's Department of Regulation

concepts.name: Financial Inclusion Mandate and Rationale
key_dimensions: Primary objective: extending banking services to migrant workers, low-income households, and unbanked populations
Connects to Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) ecosystem and last-mile delivery
Use of mobile technology as the primary delivery channel — 'mobile-first' design
Nachiket Mor Committee's 'Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low Income Households' — the policy document linkage

concepts.name: Operational Track Record: Successes and Failures
key_dimensions: Of 11 original licensees (2015), several surrendered licenses or failed to commence: Cholamandalam, Sun Pharma, FINO Paytech (initially), Telenor, Tech Mahindra — exits are examinable
Currently operational examples: Airtel Payments Bank, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB), Paytm Payments Bank (license cancelled 2024), Fino Payments Bank, Jio Payments Bank
Paytm Payments Bank cancellation (2024) by RBI — regulatory action, KYC violations, data sharing with parent — contemporary angle
India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) — government-owned, uses post office network — unique model worth noting

concepts.name: Paytm Payments Bank Cancellation (2024) — Regulatory Action
key_dimensions: RBI directed Paytm Payments Bank to stop accepting deposits/top-ups from March 2024 — specific regulatory action
Reasons: persistent non-compliance, KYC violations, and data sharing with parent entity One97 Communications
Demonstrates RBI's supervisory authority and 'fit and proper' criteria enforcement
Broader lesson: technology-driven banks face unique compliance risks — data governance as a regulatory concern

concepts.name: India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) — Unique Model
key_dimensions: Government-owned (100% GoI stake via Department of Posts) — only government-owned payments bank
Leverages 1.36 lakh post offices and 3 lakh+ postmen as delivery agents — largest physical network
Doorstep banking using postmen with micro-ATMs and smartphones — innovative last-mile model
Connects DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) delivery to rural beneficiaries — policy linkage with welfare schemes

concepts.name: Comparison: Payments Banks vs. Small Finance Banks (SFBs)
key_dimensions: Both are 'differentiated banks' under RBI's framework — common origin, different mandates
SFBs CAN lend (mandatory 75% to PSL sectors); Payments Banks CANNOT lend — the fundamental difference
Deposit ceiling: Payments Banks (Rs. 2 lakh); SFBs have no individual cap
Minimum capital: Payments Banks (Rs. 100 cr); SFBs (Rs. 200 cr) — frequently confused in exams
Conversion pathway: SFBs can upgrade to universal banks; Payments Banks have a defined path to SFB status after 5 years

concepts.name: Conversion Pathway: Payments Bank to Small Finance Bank or Universal Bank
key_dimensions: RBI guidelines (2021) allow payments banks to convert to SFBs after 5 years of satisfactory operation
Conditions: minimum net worth of Rs. 200 crore, clean regulatory track record, profitability
Fino Payments Bank has publicly explored this pathway — live example
No direct upgrade path to universal bank; must pass through SFB stage — the sequencing is an examnable nuance

concepts.name: Profitability Challenges of Payments Banks
key_dimensions: Revenue model constrained: earn from transaction fees, float income on government securities, and distribution of third-party products
Cannot earn net interest margin (NIM) from lending — the primary revenue source of banks is absent
High operating costs of technology infrastructure vs. thin fee income — sustainability concern
Most payments banks have struggled to achieve profitability — policy question of viability of the model

concepts.name: Interoperability and UPI Integration
key_dimensions: Payments banks are full members of the UPI ecosystem — can issue UPI handles (@airtel, @postpaid, etc.)
Interoperability with commercial banks through NPCI's infrastructure — IMPS, NEFT, RTGS access
Role in Aadhaar-enabled Payment System (AePS) — biometric-based transactions for rural users
Cannot operate their own ATM network extensively — must rely on shared ATM networks (NFS)

concepts.name: Know Your Customer (KYC) and Regulatory Compliance Norms
key_dimensions: Subject to the same KYC/AML (Anti-Money Laundering) norms as commercial banks under PMLA, 2002
E-KYC using Aadhaar OTP/biometric — enabled for rapid customer onboarding at scale
Video KYC (V-CIP) permitted — technology-driven compliance adaptation
Paytm case highlights consequences of KYC non-compliance — regulatory risk dimension

concepts.name: Third-Party Product Distribution as Revenue Source
key_dimensions: Permitted to distribute third-party financial products: mutual funds, insurance, pension products (as agents)
Acts as a Corporate Agent for insurance — regulated by IRDAI simultaneously, creating a dual regulatory interface
Can offer NPS (National Pension System) services as Point of Presence (PoP)
This cross-selling is the primary business model diversification strategy given lending restrictions

concepts.name: Regulatory Architecture: RBI's Role and Oversight
key_dimensions: Licensed under Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (Section 22) — NOT under RBI Act, 1934 (a common confusion)
RBI issues guidelines, conducts on-site/off-site inspections under the SPARC framework
Payments Council of India (PCI) — industry body, NOT a regulator; distinction matters
Deposit Insurance: deposits in payments banks ARE covered by DICGC up to Rs. 5 lakh — often forgotten, creates false sense that they are uninsured

concepts.name: DICGC Coverage and Depositor Protection
key_dimensions: Deposits in payments banks are insured by DICGC (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation) up to Rs. 5 lakh per depositor
DICGC covers: savings, current, fixed, recurring deposits — all deposit types across member banks including payments banks
Since deposit ceiling is Rs. 2 lakh, effectively 100% of deposits are protected — this is a unique feature worth noting
DICGC Amendment Act, 2021 — mandated timeline-based payout of insured amount — connects to recent legislative change
